passage:
Wednesday, late.
I blew up today. On the client call, in the shared chat, I typed: "Some of us actually deliver on time." Everyone saw it. Seema's camera went off. The client asked, very politely, if we could reschedule.
The thing is, I have said nothing since March. Not about the logo files, not about the report, not about the demo that slid twice. Every time I told myself it wasn't worth a fight and we should keep the peace. My hands were shaking as I typed, and part of me wanted it to hurt.
Now Seema won't answer my messages, the client is unsure of us, and the real problem is still not discussed.
Tomorrow I owe an apology for how I said it.
— Pankaj

qa.a: Pankaj was full of built-up resentment: months of silence, shaking hands and wanting the message to hurt show it.

qa.q: What could Pankaj have done earlier instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Pankaj could have raised one missed deadline privately soon after it happened, in calm words, so the problem stayed small.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when the message appeared in front of the client?
qa.a: Seema was probably embarrassed and hurt, since the first sign of any problem came in public; the camera going off hints at it, though it is not proof.

passage:
Ojas and Tarun ran a small cold-storage booking service for onion farmers from a room above a tractor showroom in the kasba. Tarun was supposed to send the weekly booking lists to the storage owners every Monday. Since the monsoon he had missed seven out of eleven Mondays. Ojas sent them himself each time, late at night, and said nothing. It wasn't worth a fight, he told himself.
In October, on a speaker call with the biggest storage owner in the area, Tarun said, "We'll have the list by Tuesday." Ojas heard himself say, loudly, "Like you had it every other week? I've been doing your job since July!"
The line went silent. The storage owner coughed and said he would call back. He didn't, for three weeks. Tarun didn't speak to Ojas for two days.

qa.q: How many Mondays had Tarun missed?
qa.a: Seven out of eleven Mondays since the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he blurted it out on the call?
qa.a: Months of built-up resentment burst out of Ojas, likely followed quickly by embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Ojas have done instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Raised the missed Mondays with Tarun privately after the first two and agreed on a fix or a backup.

qa.q: How did the storage owner react?
qa.a: The storage owner was uncomfortable, coughed, and didn't call back for three weeks, so the business lost trust.

grounding: It shows a co-founder keeping quiet about a partner's missed deadlines until resentment explodes during a client call, damaging the work and their trust.
